question: to the Commission Michał Dworczyk (ECR) Subject:

The European Union has repeatedly stated its intention to phase out Russian fossil fuels entirely and to curb the Russian Federation’s revenues from energy exports. However, even though successive rounds of sanctions have been adopted, there are still sectors and economic activities that have not been subject to appropriate restrictions, enabling Russia to generate further revenue. A particular cause for concern are media reports about a European shipyard providing repair and maintenance services for Arc7-class LNG icebreakers, which are crucial to the operation of Russia’s Yamal LNG project1. These vessels are the cornerstone of Russia’s Arctic LNG exports. Carrying out maintenance work in 2026 will extend the life of the vessels concerned by several more years, enabling Russia to continue exporting LNG and financing the war against Ukraine. In the light of the foregoing: 1.

Does the Commission take the view that the provision by EU companies of repair and maintenance services for vessels that are a key part of Russia’s LNG export infrastructure is in line with the objectives of the EU’s sanctions policy?

Does the Commission intend to propose, as part of the next round of sanctions, an amendment to Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 by removing the transition period for the provision of technical, repair and certification services for Arc7-class LNG icebreakers, in order to prevent Russia from prolonging its ability to export LNG from the Arctic?

answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.8.2026) The Commission remains fully committed to the EU’s restrictive measures (‘sanctions’) imposed in response to Russia’s illegal war of aggression against Ukraine. The 21 EU sanctions packages on Russia, with the last one adopted on 23 July 2026, include a broad range of measures in the field of energy, e.g. import ban on oil and measures targeting Russian liquified natural gas (LNG). In addition, the EU adopted, as part of the 20th sanctions package on 23 April 20261, a prohibition on maintenance services for Russian LNG tankers and icebreakers. This prohibits – after relevant wind-down periods – EU operators’ support to Russian LNG exports and further constrains Russia’s ability to maintain its seaborne assets. EU operators are prohibited since April 2026 to provide technical or financial assistance, which also covers maintenance and repairs, to Russian owned, managed, flagged or operated ice-breaker vessels and LNG tankers. The prohibition to provide services to any LNG tankers used in Russia applies from 1 January 2027. The Council may decide, in unanimity, on the possible extension of any restrictive measures, including limiting the transition period. Restrictive measures are established via Council decisions in the area of Common Foreign and Security Policy and Council regulations giving effect to those decisions in EU law. Member States are responsible for the effective implementation and enforcement of sanctions, and the Commission is closely monitoring and supporting the Member States in those tasks.
